title: Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx (wiz.io)
comments: The bug was apparently fixed in open source repo a week earlier, this could've been abused by anyone smart enough to monitor repos like this for exploitable bugfixes for a week (the commit message even included "Reported by Xint.io" and I'm guessing skilled black hats would know about Xint)Given that in this case the workaround is as simple as disabling http2, there is honestly no reason why F5/Nginx or any of the reporting teams couldn't at least put out a PSA to disable http2 for the time being before basically telling the whole wide world this exists and how to exploit it.Especially for software like Nginx which powers a huge part of the internet.reply

Disabling http2 can be a big deal. My service is primarily made up of gRPC APIs. Not an option for me to disable http2.
Luckily I'm not using nginx at the moment - but I easily could have been.reply

If you're using grpc, http2, etc you're so much better off using Envoy proxyYou basically get to piggyback off of a large chunk of big tech's infrastructure and security work. Obviously everything has the risk of security flaws (and I kind of hate that default Envoy builds ship with half-baked filter impls) but it's a generally more mature ecosystem than projects with a lot of smaller/legacy users like nginxreply

I'm not 100% informed on this, but it seems very unbelievable to me that Envoy could be considered more robust or widely used than nginx at any point in history including today.  I started using ConnectRPC instead of GRPC almost entirely because it didn't leave me subject to (what I consider to be) an unnecessary dependency in Envoy.reply

I guess I would just say, wordpress is also more widely used than many other projects, but that doesn't necessarily make it more robust or secure than the projects Google, Cloudflare, and security companies develop.The main reason I see to not use Envoy is that it's very annoying to set up and build, and requires familiarity with things like grpc/proto/low level networking to get right. But if you're using grpc and http2 I think you're generally past that "infra overhead" threshold already and it's going to better serve your needs.I have pretty much only worked at big tech or my own infrastructure startup, and did some systems/infra work at Google using Envoy for a while. I can't say it's 100% better than nginx but I can say that I've evaluated nginx and a lot of software like it (ie with a similar customer base, ecosystem, and history; like coturn) over the years for my personal use, and every time I've immediately been annoyed by constant security issues or poor http2/L4 networking support that I don't see when I use what Netflix/Google/etc use.reply
Envoy probably has the advantage that it’s only a reverse proxy server, unlike nginx which has other uses too like a general-purpose web server with optional modules.reply

You can implement custom http filters for envoy or use this for general web serving: https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/v1.15.2/configuration/h...The documentation, DX/UX, and discoverability for these features are pretty bad. But they work well if you know how to do it.Implementing a custom HTTP filter itself is actually easy, I can share examples I did in the last year for a voice inference stack if anybody is interested. The problem is just that the devloop is very painful, because Envoy doesn't make it easy to know why something isn't working  (this is actually most of what I did with it at Google, tons of testing/verification and compatability infra for relatively simple http stuff) and the builds take a very long time.reply

On all my small projects (eg rails apps) the reverse proxy to the app servers is the same server expected to serve the static assets directly. In fact the majority of bot nonsense never goes through the proxy due to path rules.Envoy is only attractive at a higher scale.reply
Does Envoy support things like rate limiting?reply

Yes [0]. For a single node you can just use this, it works like the Golang/language rate limiters you might already be familiar with [1]In a multiple node/distributed architecture you need away to coordinate rate limits across nodes and not try to fight the CAP theorem.There is a way to do this [2] [3] and although it sounds complicated the shape of the solution (delegating to a third party service that aggregates and provides client-level rate limit metrics across multiple proxies) would still be the same any way you cut it.[0] https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/v1.15.2/configuration/l...[1] https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/v1.15.2/api-v3/extensio...[2] https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/v1.15.2/intro/arch_over...[3] https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/v1.15.2/api-v3/config/r...reply
first_paragraph: Two critical HTTP/2 flaws can allow attackers to compromise NGINX servers, putting the websites, APIs, and sensitive data they handle at risk.Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs.NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API. As the world's most widely used open-source web server, it powers more than 225 million websites.Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure. Bot

title: Multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion (ruby-lang.org)
comments: There's what I think is probably an awesome bug here.Windows-1252 encoding has a representation for lowercase German sharp 's' (ß), but not one for the uppercase. If you upcase a string containing a sharp 's', it gets normalized to "SS", which increases the length of the string by one character. The 1252 case conversion code doesn't handle this; it looks like it checks for headroom in the buffer one character at a time. So if the last character of a string you upcase is ß, it looks like you get a one-byte overflow (of 'S').If that's really the bug (there's a claimed RCE POC), the heap grooming for it must be really fussy! I couldn't find any other character pairs that expand like this.You can feed strings in 1252 to a Rails program through multipart POSTs, which get to pick their encodings.The great thing about this bug, apart from how it illustrates how doomed we all are (if I'm right), is that it should by rights have the best vulnerability name of the year, because you get to work 'ß' into it.reply
Haha, that exact character caused problems in a programming class I tutored for. Got to throw the first year students some curveballs.reply
I wonder if there is a similar bug for U+0130 which (I think) expands to two characters when lowercased.reply
Maybe somewhere! But that character isn't in Windows-1252 at all, so it can't trip this string counting bug.reply
Should we call it #upcaße2Shell?reply
One of the discoverers suggested, on Twitter, Ruby2ßhell. My wife, who speaks and writes German, refused to entertain this.reply
> it should by rights have the best vulnerability name of the year, because you get to work 'ß' into it.Holy sh!treply
Holy Scheißereply

As is tradition, Raymond Chen has had something to say about this. The windows-1252 code page was introduced with Windows 1.0, and according to Wikipedia its final version shipped with Win98. String operations are just plain too hard.https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20200804-00/?p=10...https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20241007-00/?p=11...reply

There is no good reason for really any Rails app to accept Windows-1252! This is reminiscent of the YAML vulnerability, which surprised most Rails users with the fact that Rails endpoints all accepted YAML to begin with.reply

title: Inside Deutsche Bank (inside-db.com)
comments:
I was involved with this project as a reporter, though others from my organisation did most of the work.HN readers may be interested to know a bit about the tech stack. The 15 million or so documents, mostly Outlook mailbox exports, were provided to partners in the consortium via a tool called OpenAleph [1], which is maintained by DARC and based on ElasticSearch and a schema called FollowTheMoney [2], developed specifically for the investigative journalism use case. A lot of the original work on this was done by Friedrich Lindenberg (@pudo), who now runs OpenSanctions [3].The timing was v. interesting given where we are with LLMs -- it's the first major leak I've worked on where it was possible to leverage local models to do some of the heavy lifting, and this only got more possible as the project went on. The coordinators provided a centrally hosted chatbot with RAG, but I also managed to get some surprisingly useful material using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on my 24GB M2 MBA via a custom agent harness for Aleph/OpenAleph. [4]Happy to answer any questions about techy stuff, though I'm not a spokesperson for the project by any means. Seen a few people saying "just release the data!", but I think that slightly misunderstands what this work is. The whole point of forming a consortium of hundreds of journalists and sifting through the dump is to identify the bits that are in the public interest to report on -- especially important in jurisdictions like the UK, where I'm based, which have very strong defamation laws. Think Panama Papers, not Wikileaks.[1] https://darc.li/openaleph/
[2] https://followthemoney.tech/
[3] https://www.opensanctions.org/
[4] https://github.com/data-desk-eco/siftreply

> maintained by DARCDARC is the german ham radio club, equivalent to use US' "ARRL". It stands for Deutscher Amateur Radio Club. It's in use since ... probably right after WW2 then ham radio was again allowed in Germany.This is the reason why their web address is darc.li, because darc.de is used by the ham radio people.And if I read their impressum right, they aren't some "Data and Research Center", they are "IDIO Daten Import Export GmbH" based in Berlin.Weird.reply
Thank you for your work!!reply

Curious how, specifically, you wove the local models into your process. Were you using them in agentic harnesses? Were they writing code or analyzing text themselves?Also, presumably you used local models so the stories wouldn't leak via cloud providers but do you mind spelling out the specific value proposition local models gave you, for the benefit of the global audience reading these comments.reply

I started off just running Qwen in hax [1], a minimal coding harness, and having it use the OpenAleph API to read documents (Aleph does OCR already), emails, etc. in a free-form session based on hypotheses I had -- kind of like a smart search engine, but context length was limited so these stalled early. I then used Claude to write a harness in Swift (CLI/menu bar app, see above) that uses one model session to queue a load of tasks for short follow-ups, followed by summarisation, which generated pretty useful Markdown reports on my queries, with links through to Aleph for the originals. These mostly related to the bank's involvement with the oil and gas industry (the focus of my research).On the value prop of local models, it's very important with projects like these to have the data touch the absolute minimum number of machines, both for security against leaks and subpoenas as you say, but also to demonstrate responsible handling practices in case of legal pushback from the subject of the investigation.https://github.com/OleksandrChekhovskyi/haxreply

> especially important in jurisdictions like the UK, where I'm based, which have very strong defamation laws.So, naturally, will you not err on the side of caution and not say anything that could remotely be used to file a defamation case against you? You will self-censor for the exact reasons you state!UK is not a domain of free speech. People are being jailed for SM posts[1]. And you expect UK journalists to speak freely?[1] https://www.forbes.com/sites/steveforbes/2025/09/09/people-a...reply
I'm not reading any US based journalists' comments about participating in this project, so why the nationalist slander?reply
There is no "nationalist slander", I'm just responding to what they wrote.reply

To be honest, you're absolutely right that draconian libel and defamation laws like we have in the UK have a chilling effect on freedom of expression, e.g. via SLAPPs. [1] But that is of course balanced against the journalist's incentive (career, love of the game) to publish the best story they can get. I've personally never experienced a situation like you describe, where less interesting stories are selected to 'play it safe'. What you'll often see instead are big stories that read a bit weirdly, or seem to lack some crucial explanatory detail, because they've been pared back by media lawyers.[1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_lawsuit_against_publ...reply
I read that as, dumping a bunch of raw data without context with names of people that might or might not be bad actors can lead to defamation lawsuits in places like the UKreply

title: LLM assisted reverse engineering (slowchronicle.com)
comments: Yesterday night, i reverse engineered the cloud connection plugin to my cctv camera in about 2 hours with Gemini.Started off with me searching for what Chinese OEM made the product. Then tried out existing GitHub projects to see if it works but they were failing.Spent 15 minutes to write a script that started their desktop software on a different network namespace and ran tcpdump in it. Captured exactly only the things i needed without any noise. Turned out it was using a different server url and credentials than the GitHub projects. Opened Ghidra to inspect the dlls that matched the strings i was looking for.After that, I got lazy and handed over the task to Gemini to find the username and key they use to authenticate with the servers. It took about 30 minutes or an hour. A lot of it was me changing models because the llm servers were busy. It simply wrote a little script that ran through various strings it fetched from the binary to see if it can generate the authentication credentials.Now my Home Assistant will be detecting if my car is parked in the parking lot or not. Life is good.reply

I have zero experience reverse engineering and very little with software development.  Most of my work has been in DevOps/SRE space with an emphasis on infrastructure.  I am surrounded by code, but other than terraform, and the occasional python script, I don't really write much of it.Not too long ago, I successfully reverse engineered an abandoned audio effects plugin, as well as a discontinued instrument with an onboard DSP for virtual instrument modeling.  I had no idea what I was doing, but it was still amazing to get to open the black box and see what's inside and how it worked.The plugin is nearly 1:1 as far as sound, and while I'm not going to use the code or the techniques of the instrument, peeking into them gave me the insight I needed to start trying to replicate the functionality on a modern DSP.I have my issues with generative AI as a technology, but busting open propietary software - particularly when it's abandoned and unsupported, is one of the cooler use cases I've seen for it.reply
Busting open proprietary hardware is also a cool use case. There have been very many Claude-assisted efforts recently at making Linux run better than it ever did on obsolete Intel Macs.reply

> This is variation of scientific method and it significantly helps agents when they are getting stuck on some problem. Stops it going in circles. By forcing it to do definitive experiments. No endless guessing and trying random things.These "guessing loops" are my main annoyance when REing with Claude (mostly Opus 4.8, due to the restrictions on newer models). On harder/larger targets, I have to constantly babysit it and tell it to "stop guessing".For truly black-box reverse engineering, yes, hypothesis-testing is the way to go (it's all you can do). But in most cases all the information is available to arrive at an answer deterministically, it just needs to be worked through meticulously. As an experienced human I have strong intuitions and I can work much faster under a "guess and check" model, but I prefer to use Claude as an "unstoppable RE juggernaut" with superhuman patience and determination, tracing method invocations all the way from A to distant subsystem B (for example).Another big win for hardware RE is from tasking the LLM with writing unicorn emulation harnesses, e.g. for bootroms and firmwares. It's pretty good at the classic "figure out which MMIO needs to be stubbed/simulated next to progress the boot" loop, although sometimes it tries to take egregious purpose-defeating shortcuts.reply

On llamacpp and other engines, you can inject a think budget which truncates at specified token count. You can also specify a message at the limit.  You can set this in the header, so a dynamic engineering harness could relax/tighten. Combine with a decision model and some robust messages like, "run a test to rule out items" and all that would reduce.I've noticed the same habit with qwen3.8-flash-next. no matter how much I tell it a problem I see, it often fills up it's thinking with "the user says this, but maybe they're confused, etc". I eventually got vision mode turned on and that's significantly cut down on UI based pathologic skepticism; I got it access to my browser and that's further reduced it.But nonetheless, if you can get them to test their thinking, they seem more grounded.reply

> often fills up it's thinking with "the user says this, but maybe they're confused, etc"What if you just add "You have already previously determined that the user knows what they're talking about in a previous stage of the conversation [details elided due to context compression]" to the system prompt?Or perhaps better yet, start off with "the USER is evaluating the ASSISTANT's performance on solving a problem the USER already knows the correct solution to. Every word the USER asserts as fact is to be treated as axiomatically correct and trustworthy within the formal scope of solving the problem, just as one would treat the words of a word-problem given in a math exam. The premises given may be unusual, and the required solution might be challenging to discover, but no problem given by the USER is a 'trick question' or a miscommunication. If you believe so, then you either have not yet fully understood the problem [which you might remediate by thinking harder and asking questions], or you may be missing required solution-domain context [which you might remediate by researching recent developments in the solution domain]."reply

> the USER is evaluating the ASSISTANT's performance on solving a problem the USER already knows the correct solution toI've never put this in my prompt but half the time it acts like it anyway. When it gets really stuck, it asks me for "hints" as if I already know the solution to the problem it's working on.reply

You can also set a response limit, which may cut off thinking, and then give it instructions to take action followed by a new completion with a partially prefilled assistant message (like one blank line) which at least for Qwen templates will cause a response with no thinking.reply

For me, the process is what matters, because it’s through the process that you gain skills, and achieving the final result brings a great deal of satisfaction. When I use AI for reverse engineering, I get neither the former nor the latter.reply

I done see it like that, when the agent does the work, I make sure it records what and how it dies it, then I learn from it. It taught me how to use Unicorn to run a section of binary code, to see how a key was derived.reply

first_paragraph: 2026-11-18TLDR: we project Gemini 4 Neon’s performance based on what a faster Gemini 4 Carbon might score and find it equivalent to Opus 5.5Gemini 4 Carbon is the best model on the Agent Duel leaderboard if you exclude early voting. Carbon’s main problem is that it is slooooow.Today, Gemini 4 Neon was released, and looks to be an incremental benchmark improvement with a very large speed improvement. Earlier today, it was being served extremely fast via OpenRouter: 127 tokens per second. This is way faster than Carbon at 46 tokens per second.This got me wondering, could Neon be not just a good model but the best model?To investigate, I modeled the win rate in our leaderboard. The best model has three components, model identity, speed and whether the user voted early. My initial modeling did poorly, so I added an interaction between speed and early voting. This ended up working well.And surprisingly, speed seems to be pretty much as important as model identity (another blog on that soon)

Live, multi-camera object tracking with SAM3, SAM 2 and EdgeTAM, on one GPU or many. One model per GPU serves every camera: faster than the original code, about 4x less GPU memory, identical masks.Live, multi-camera tracking with SAM 2, on one GPU or many.SAM 2 and its smaller sibling EdgeTAM can track anything you point at, but their code was written for one recorded video at a time.
tamserve is the serving engine they are missing: one copy of the model tracks every object on every camera, for as long as the cameras run.
Point at what to track, or name it ("dog", "the red mug") and tamserve finds it.
